BOOK I.


ARGUMENT.[1]


THE WRATH OF NOBODY.


In the war of Toyland, the heroes having quarreled over a trifle,
withdraw in anger from the field. The gods debate the matter at
length, and nothing at all is resolved.
    The time of one single day is taken up in this book.


Achilles' wrath, to Greece the direful spring[2]
Of woes unnumber'd, heavenly goddess, sing!
That wrath which hurl'd to Pluto's gloomy reign
The souls of mighty chiefs untimely slain.

[Illustration: ] HOMER INVOKING THE MUSE


Declare, O Muse! in what ill-fated hour
Sprung the fierce strife, from what offended power.[3]
Latona's son a dire contagion spread,
And heap'd the camp with mountains of the dead.


BOOK II.


The trial of the army, and catalogue of the toy forces. Jupiter, in
pursuance of the request of Thetis, sends a deceitful vision to
Agamemnon, persuading him to lead the army to battle.


Now night, the various hue of shifting fate,
On heaven's proud arches roll'd the wheel of state;
While Jove, revolving in his mind the vow
Paid to the sacred head of great Achilles now.


CONCLUDING NOTE.


We have now passed through the Tiny Epic, and seen the anger of
Nobody, and the terrible effects of it, at an end.


 [1] What, says the editor, is the natural root of this quarrel?

 [2] The direful spring: Buckley notes this as a strong opening.

 [3] Offended power: a reference to Apollo, priest-avenger.
